citation: Mansikka, Jan-Erik (2009 [published online 30 September 2008]). Can Boredom Educate Us? Tracing a Mood in Heidegger's Fundamental Ontology from an Educational Point of View. Studies in Philosophy and Education, 28, 255-268. DOI 10.1007/s11217-008-9116-0.
discipline: philosophy of education (Heidegger studies; phenomenology of Stimmung/boredom); no empirical, affective-science, or attention-science content, though the source's own abstract and opening paragraph explicitly invoke Csikszentmihalyi's 'flow' as a named contrast pole
thesis: Reading Heidegger's phenomenology of boredom from The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics (1929/30), with supporting reference to Being and Time's Befindlichkeit and What is Metaphysics?'s nothingness, as a resource for education: boredom's phenomenology contains 'transformative potentialities' that can illuminate our cultural situation as a whole, and turning away from boredom is always also a possibility of turning away from ourselves. The paper's organizing move reads Heidegger's three phenomenologically distinguished forms of boredom (situative/first, self-forming-emptiness/second, profound/third) as correlating with three modes of (un)meaningful learning -- meaningless/technical instruction, engaged-but-inauthentic performance-learning, and profound boredom as a site of possible pedagogical rupture -- before turning, in a final movement, to profound boredom's connection to authenticity, waiting, and a non-Platonic 'Socratic Method' of teaching.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Opens on the flow/boredom contrast (Csikszentmihalyi 1990) and the everyday, evaluative sense in which boredom and interest function as a coincidentia oppositorum registering how situations 'matter to us'; raises the pedagogical and existential questions (lack-of-interest vs. teacher failure vs. self-responsibility) the paper answers via Heidegger.

sections.title: The Concept of Boredom
sections.summary: Traces a conceptual history: medieval acedia as a spiritual disorder of 'too little love' (Aquinas via Raposa); the romantic 'expressive subject' for whom boredom signals a distorted relation to the infinite (Svendsen); the modern reduction of boredom to an individual psychological/physiological disorder, rejected as unable to explain boredom's relation to world-experience; boredom reframed as strictly relational, tied to (lack of) meaningfulness (Raposa).

sections.title: Moods as a Fundamental Way of Being-in-the-World
sections.summary: Establishes Stimmung and Befindlichkeit as existentials disclosing Dasein's Being-in-the-world 'as a whole' prior to any subject/object split; notes anxiety (BT), nothingness (What is Metaphysics?), and boredom (FCM) as Heidegger's three sustained fundamental-mood analyses; 'philosophy in each case happens in a fundamental mood.'

sections.title: Heidegger and the Experience of Boredom
sections.summary: Compressed three-part exposition, each closed by Mansikka's own Being/Time diagram: (a) situative/first-form boredom via the railway-station example (held in delay by dragging time, left empty by things offering nothing); (b) self-forming-emptiness/second-form boredom via the evening-invitation example (boredom concentrating on us, time spent and lost, the stretched 'now'); (c) profound/third-form boredom (total indifference, telling refusal of beings as a whole, the rupturing Augenblick, credited to Kierkegaard).

sections.title: Three Ways of (not) Learning and Being Bored -- A Learning that is Not Meaningful
sections.summary: Maps first-form boredom onto technical, 'objectivistic' instruction that brackets lived experience (via Being and Time's account of theoretical looking, and Egan's account of enthusiasm and wonder).

sections.title: Three Ways of (not) Learning and Being Bored -- A Learning that is Meaningful but Leaves Us Empty
sections.summary: Maps second-form boredom onto engaged-yet-inauthentic learning: the fully occupied, even high-achieving, student governed by das Man (the 'they-self') rather than an authentic self-relation.

sections.title: Three Ways of (not) Learning and Being Bored -- Beyond Learning and Waiting
sections.summary: Reaches for profound boredom's educational potential via the recovered 'essence of paideia' (quoted from Heidegger via Thomson 2003), Biesta's account of the educator's 'responsibility for what is to come,' Dasein's waiting as a keeping-to-itself, and a 'modern version of the Socratic Method... without platonic metaphysical assumptions'; closes with Fromm on Calvinist activity as escape from anxiety.

sections.title: Epilogue
sections.summary: Surveys shared Christian/Buddhist ambivalence about indifference and emptiness (Raposa); reads profound boredom via Agamben as Heidegger's 'anthropogenesis' and via Svendsen as an 'initiation to metaphysics'; connects Heidegger's implicit counter-education (Gur-Ze'ev) to Foucauldian power, critical pedagogy (Giroux & McLaren), and Greene's 'opening the world'; closes with a cultural critique of the entertainment industry's flight from boredom, quoting Heidegger's 'absence of distress'/'smug contentment' diagnosis, and insists emancipation is effortful and non-linear.

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)
constructs.treatment: genuinely and substantially treated: exposited (indifference, telling refusal, Augenblick) and made the pedagogical center of gravity (paideia, waiting, entertainment critique)

constructs.label: being-bored-by (1st form)
constructs.treatment: genuinely treated via the railway-station example; transposed onto meaningless/technical instruction

constructs.label: being-bored-with (2nd form)
constructs.treatment: genuinely treated via the evening-invitation example; transposed onto engaged-but-inauthentic, they-self-governed learning

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: false friend: Mansikka's own label 'situative boredom' for the first form invites confusion with the psychometric state/trait distinction, but the contrast is strictly phenomenological (situation-bound vs. arising from Dasein itself), never an individual-differences claim -- not counted as a genuine hit

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: not treated; no psychometric or individual-differences claim of any kind appears

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: false friend: 'slipping away from ourselves toward whatever is happening' (second form) superficially resembles attentional drift but is an ontological claim about self-abandonment to das Man, not a claim about task-unrelated cognitive content -- not counted

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: not treated; the source's register is ontological/existential throughout, never attentional-cognitive

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: genuinely but loosely treated as a philosophical analog: boredom (especially profound boredom) 'wishes to tell us something... not something arbitrary or contingent' and has 'transformative potentialities' -- an existential-hermeneutic disclosure claim, not an empirical adaptive/regulatory-function claim; flagged for register

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: genuinely and explicitly treated: Csikszentmihalyi's Flow (1990) named as boredom's contrast pole in the paper's own opening paragraph

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: genuinely and substantially treated: technical/objectivistic instruction; Egan's 'desiccated and devoid of energy and life' education; the entertainment-industry's meaning-flattening amusement

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: genuinely and substantially treated: Langeweile ('long while') etymology; dragging time and being held in delay; the stretched 'now' without past or future; entrancement and the Augenblick

readings.claim: Boredom and interest are evaluative registers of how situations, events, and activities 'matter to us,' applicable to educational situations no less than any other.
Boredom is a strictly relational, not intrinsic, property -- nothing is boring 'in itself' -- drawn from Raposa to set up Heidegger's Dasein-analytic.
Fundamental moods are existentials that disclose Being-in-the-world 'as a whole' prior to any subject/object split; they are not 'added' to experience after the fact but make experience possible.

Heidegger's three forms of boredom progressively deepen the same two structural moments (being-left-empty, being-held-in-delay) toward pure temporality, culminating in profound boredom's 'telling refusal' of beings as a whole.

[Mansikka's own extension] There is a workable correlation between the three forms of boredom and three modes of (un)meaningful learning: meaningless/technical rote instruction, engaged-but-inauthentic performance-learning under das Man, and profound boredom as a possible site of pedagogical rupture toward authenticity.
An objectivistic, purely theoretical educational stance that brackets lived experience can increase rather than dissolve meaninglessness and boredom.

A student can be outwardly exemplary -- fully engaged, high-achieving -- while remaining inauthentic in Heidegger's technical sense, because das Man rather than the student's own self is making the decisions that matter.

Mansikka explicitly disclaims prescribing induced profound boredom as an educational method; the claim is only that education's over-arching goal should cultivate a 'responsive hermeneutic receptivity' leading students back to themselves.
Genuine education, on Heidegger's gloss of Plato's paideia (quoted via Thomson 2003), 'lays hold of the soul itself' rather than depositing information into an empty vessel.

The contemporary entertainment/amusement industry functions as a structural mechanism for continuously 'driving away' boredom, foreclosing the possibility of confronting one's 'innermost possibilities.'

Heidegger's own diagnosis of contemporary Dasein's 'absence of distress,' masked by 'smug contentment in not being endangered' (FCM Ch.5/section 38a; cf. fcm-07), directly underwrites Mansikka's educational-cultural critique of busyness and entertainment.

concepts.term: telling refusal (Versagen) of beings as a whole
modern Socratic Method (without platonic metaphysical assumptions)

interlocutors.name: Csikszentmihalyi, Mihaly
interlocutors.role: external, non-cluster interlocutor: 'flow' cited by name as boredom's contrast pole in the opening paragraph, not developed further

interlocutors.name: Aquinas, Thomas
interlocutors.role: medieval theology of acedia as spiritual disorder ('too little love'), cited via Raposa

interlocutors.name: Svendsen, Lars Fr. H.
interlocutors.role: romantic conception of boredom and the expressive subject; cited repeatedly on Langeweile, the second-form 'meaning-filled' analysis, and boredom as 'initiation to metaphysics'

interlocutors.name: Raposa, Michael L.
interlocutors.role: Boredom and the Religious Imagination: relational concept of boredom, plenitude/emptiness of bored time, Christian/Buddhist ambivalence about indifference

interlocutors.name: Braque, Remi
interlocutors.role: concept of 'world' as inhabited experience, not perceptual object

interlocutors.name: Svenaeus, Fredrik
interlocutors.role: Heideggers stamningsbegrepp: moods as presuppositions for thinking and action prior to re-presentation

interlocutors.name: Egan, Kieran
interlocutors.role: Romantic Understanding: enthusiasm and wonder as vital educational attitudes; 'desiccated and devoid of energy and life' quoted

interlocutors.name: Biesta, Gert J. J.
interlocutors.role: Beyond Learning: the educator's 'responsibility for what is to come,' undertaken without foreknowledge of that future

interlocutors.name: Thomson, Iain (cited as 'Thomson 2003')
interlocutors.role: source of the Plato paideia quotation; near-certain reprint/republication of this cluster's bor-sec-19 (Thomson 2001, Inquiry) as a chapter in Peters (ed.) 2003

interlocutors.name: Fromm, Erich
interlocutors.role: The Fear of Freedom: Calvinist activity as a desperate escape from doubt and powerlessness, not inner strength

interlocutors.name: Agamben, Giorgio
interlocutors.role: The Open: profound boredom as a description of Heidegger's 'anthropogenesis,' the becoming-Dasein

interlocutors.name: Kierkegaard, Soren
interlocutors.role: credited origin of the Augenblick concept Heidegger draws on for profound boredom's rupture

interlocutors.name: Foucault, Michel
interlocutors.role: power as circulating through networks of relationships, not emanating from a given point; invoked for counter-education

interlocutors.name: Giroux, Henry & McLaren, Peter
interlocutors.role: critical pedagogy: knowledge as always situated, socially transmitted, embedded in structures of power

interlocutors.name: Greene, Maxine
interlocutors.role: Releasing the Imagination: education as 'a mode of opening the world' to critical judgment and transformative action

interlocutors.name: Gur-Ze'ev, Ilan
interlocutors.role: coined/theorized 'counter-education' in relation to Heidegger, transcendence, and possibility

interlocutors.name: Peters, Michael A. (ed.)
interlocutors.role: editor of Heidegger, Education and Modernity (2003), the volume containing 'Thomson 2003' and Hogan's chapter, both cited by Mansikka

interlocutors.name: Ott, Hugo
interlocutors.role: Martin Heidegger: A Political Life; footnoted to bracket the Nazi-politics question when giving positive sense to Heidegger's 'strength and power'

tensions.axis: meaningless/technical instruction (form 1) vs. engaged-but-inauthentic performance-learning (form 2) vs. profound-boredom-as-rupture (form 3)
tensions.note: Mansikka's own three-part pedagogical typology, presented as successive depths of possible educational (un)meaningfulness rather than a strict hierarchy or causal sequence.

tensions.axis: authentic self-relation vs. das Man (they-self) in learning
tensions.note: A student's outward engagement and success (grades, participation) is compatible with governance by das Man rather than an authentic self-relation; the two axes (engagement, authenticity) are shown to be independent.

tensions.axis: objectivistic/theoretical educational stance vs. lived, experiential meaningfulness
tensions.note: A radically objectivistic stance aiming at cognitive understanding 'without moods' can produce a decrease of meaningfulness and thus boredom, rather than deeper understanding.

tensions.axis: Heidegger's philosophical claims vs. his political entanglement
tensions.note: Mansikka footnotes the 'danger' of giving positive meaning to Heidegger's 'strength and power' given his connection to Nazism (via Ott 1993), and elects to read the philosophy on a general existential-phenomenological level bracketing the political question.

tensions.axis: constant entertainment/amusement vs. profound boredom's rupture
tensions.note: The contemporary entertainment industry's continuous 'driving away' of boredom is read as foreclosing the very possibility profound boredom might otherwise open toward one's 'innermost possibilities.'

tensions.axis: competency-accumulation model of education vs. paideia as soul-transformation
tensions.note: Heidegger's critique of education as mere 'accumulation of learned competencies' (quoted, p.164) is set against the recovered paideia ideal of education as transforming the soul in its entirety.

fcm.note: The railway-station exposition of situative/first-form boredom (being held in delay by dragging time, left empty by things offering nothing) directly paraphrases fcm-04's Part One Ch.2 SS19-23 material and its two structural moments (Leergelassenheit, Hingehaltenheit); transposed educationally onto meaningless/technical instruction.

The evening-invitation exposition of self-forming-emptiness/second-form boredom (boredom concentrating on us, the stretched 'now') directly paraphrases fcm-05's Part One Ch.3 SS24-28 material; transposed educationally onto engaged-but-inauthentic, they-self-governed learning.

The profound-boredom exposition (total indifference, telling refusal of beings as a whole, the Augenblick credited to Kierkegaard) directly paraphrases fcm-06's Part One Ch.4 SS29-36 material; developed educationally via paideia, waiting, and a modernized Socratic Method.

Mansikka quotes verbatim, without naming Chapter Five, the same GA pp.244-46 passage fcm-07 identifies as SS38a's keystone diagnosis of contemporary Dasein's absence of essential oppressiveness ('learned competencies... can never be replaced', p.164; 'smug contentment in not being endangered', pp.164-166); underwrites Mansikka's critique of competency-accumulation education and the entertainment industry (P/anticipatory-application for the explicit fcm-07 cross-reference).
